chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Who owned the Savoy: liquor license and a barbecue fortune
summary: Buchanan managed the Savoy, a drugstore owner blocked its liquor license, and an Italian family made a fortune from a barbecue on 136th Street.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: When Buchanan ran the Savoy, he was just the manager.

But he was sort of a stockholder, because he was the only one that knew how to run it. But they didn't have any liquor there. The liquor was held by (what was his name?) Socks Brownstein(?)...the owner of the drugstore across the street from it... What was his name? He was the one that prevented the Savoy from getting a liquor license. For years Brownstein...Sapir...not Sapirstein... Sapirstein was then the head of...the Alcohol Lord of New York State -- later they put him out of the way. Not the head of the Harlem Globetrotters. What the hell... Oh, it was a famous name. Anyway, he was powerful enough to keep the Savoy from getting a liquor license, because he had Harlem's...
Well, when I first went there in 1937 they had sherry, they had wine, but they didn't have liquor.
I don't think they had liquor.
They finally got it later on. He still owns it, (?). I can tell you the...136th Street is the...the

Italian family had a barbecue. Nobody's ever challenged them, made a barbecue... You know, the chicken and ribs and all that. For years and years and years. And they used to give away the unwanted part of the hogs and all that to families, which was a very nice gesture, during the holidays, you know. But that man built up a tremendous fortune out of that corner. I don't know where that Italian family is today...
